title: The Bernstein–Vazirani Algorithm
summary: Find a whole secret string with one query.
objectives: Recover a hidden n-bit string with one query
Read the string from the final state, with qubit 0 as its last character
Say why a randomized classical program still needs n queries
mission: Find the hidden 4-bit string s with a single call to oracle(qc): at the end, the input register (qubits 0 to 3) must be in |s⟩. Qubit 0 is the last character of s, so s = s3 s2 s1 s0 and the state label is |q3 q2 q1 q0⟩.

prediction.question: The oracle is f(x) = s·x ⊕ 1, with a constant bias added. What does the input register end in?
options: The complement of s, because the bias flips every bit
A random string, because the bias spoils the interference
prediction.explanation: The bias multiplies every term by the same sign (−1)^b, which is a global phase. Interference between terms is unchanged and the register still ends in |s⟩ with certainty.

hints: This is the Deutsch–Jozsa circuit with four input qubits. Where does the auxiliary qubit sit?
The auxiliary qubit is qubit 4 and goes to |−⟩. The four inputs get Hadamards before and after the query.
A loop over qubits 0 to 3 with qc.h does both layers. The auxiliary is qc.x(4) then qc.h(4).

challenge.mission: Solve Bernstein–Vazirani with 4 qubits and no auxiliary qubit. The hidden oracle is now a phase oracle, phase_oracle(qc), which maps |x⟩ to (−1)^(s·x ⊕ b)|x⟩ on qubits 0 to 3 (the bias b only contributes a global phase). Call it once in a circuit qc with 4 qubits so that the register ends in |s⟩, with qubit 0 as the last character of s. The function oracle(qc) is not available.
hints: The phase oracle already writes the sign (−1)^(s·x). What did the auxiliary qubit do for you before?
Without the auxiliary qubit, what remains of the circuit?
Hadamard on every qubit, phase_oracle(qc), Hadamard on every qubit.
